sections.title: Why Creators Look for Modern PureRef Alternatives
sections.html:
While PureRef is remarkably versatile, many everyday creative workflows run into specific roadblocks with its infinite-canvas philosophy:

  • Lack of integrated, structured text scratchpads alongside image cards.
  • Heavy RAM usage when large image collections remain loaded in memory.
  • Keyboard navigation and canvas zooming that can feel disconnected from standard desktop conventions.
  • No built-in clipboard text management for code, hex codes, or prompt notes.

sections.title: Top 7 PureRef Alternatives Compared for 2026
sections.html:
We evaluated the leading reference board tools available across Windows, macOS, and Linux:

  1. FloatBoard: The premier lightweight hybrid tool combining image tiles with an always-on-top text scratchpad. 100% offline and sub-40ms latency.
  2. Kuadro: Lightweight per-image floating viewer, but lacks unified multi-card grid layouts and text notes.
  3. BeeRef: Open-source Python/Qt reference viewer, though interface customization is limited.
  4. Eagle: Powerful asset management library, but heavier footprint designed for long-term archiving rather than quick floating reference.
  5. VizRef: Solid iPad alternative for mobile illustrators.
  6. Pureref (Legacy): Still robust for massive 100+ image moodboards, though resource-heavy.
  7. Milanote: Cloud-based moodboard builder, but requires constant internet connectivity and monthly subscription fees.

This guide shows a repeatable debugging workflow and compares massCode, Pieces and Cacher for storage and retrieval.

sections.title: Start with one reproducible UI bug
sections.html:
First write down the action that triggers the bug, the viewport or window size and what actually happens. Then record the expected behavior. A screenshot without these details can look convincing but leave a teammate unable to reproduce anything.

Keep the screenshot in your issue or project folder, where it will still be available after this working session. Copy only the smallest relevant markup or CSS fragment onto your temporary board. Label it with the file path and component name so you can return to the authoritative source.

Do not paste access tokens, customer data or private URLs into a board that may appear in a screen share. Redact the screenshot before sharing it.

sections.title: Put a screenshot and code snippet side by side
sections.html:
1. Capture the visual symptom. Make one screenshot at the size where the problem appears. Keep the original in the bug report.
  2. Copy the relevant snippet. Add its file path and a brief note about why you suspect it. A text card is a reference, not a synchronized copy of the source file.
  3. Add both to FloatBoard. Put the screenshot in the image panel and the snippet plus expected result in the text panel. The image above shows this mixed layout.
  4. Pin the board beside the editor. Keep it in view while the editor and browser remain the tools you use to change and test the code.
  5. Change one likely cause and reproduce again. Replace the working note with the new observation; do not stack unexplained copies of the same snippet.

This is useful when you need a snippet manager with images for the immediate task. FloatBoard is not a searchable code library or an IDE: it does not run code, highlight syntax or keep pasted text in sync with Git.

sections.title: Example: debug an overflowing image grid at 390px
sections.html:
Suppose a gallery extends past its container on a narrow screen. The note below keeps the question, evidence and next check together. It is an illustrative checklist, not a diagnosis of FloatBoard or a universal CSS fix.

Bug: image cards overflow the gallery panel
Reproduce: open the gallery at a 390px viewport
Actual: horizontal scrolling appears
Expected: cards stay inside the panel
Source: styles/gallery.css, .gallery-grid
Evidence: screenshot saved in issue #123
Next check: grid columns, item min-width, image sizing

In DevTools, inspect the actual grid and its children. If a child cannot shrink, test whether its minimum size causes the overflow; if the column definition is fixed, test a responsive layout. Keep the before and after screenshots at the same viewport. The fix belongs in the source and its test, not in the reference note.

A clipboard manager can preserve recently copied material, including images in some products. A saved snippet adds information such as title, language and source. A floating board keeps selected material visible. These are different roles, and one app can support more than one role.

Always compare an older clip with the current source before reusing it. See the clipboard workflow for the product details.

sections.title: Questions developers ask about snippets and screenshots
sections.html:
What is the best way to organize code snippets?

Keep production code in the repository. Save genuinely reusable fragments in a searchable snippet manager with a descriptive title, language, source link and date or version. Keep temporary debugging fragments in a small task board, then remove them when the issue is resolved.

Can a clipboard manager store images?

Some can; capabilities differ by product. FloatBoard lets you add images to its visible board and has recent text clipboard history. Do not assume its history stores every image you have copied. For a screenshot you must preserve, save the original in your project or issue tracker.

Is there a free alternative to Pieces for snippets?

massCode is a free, open-source snippet library, according to its official site. FloatBoard has a limited free plan for visible text-and-image references, but is not a Pieces replacement for searchable snippets or image-to-code extraction. Compare current plans and features on each official site.

What is the best code snippet manager for Windows?

There is no single best choice for every workflow. For a searchable local library, compare massCode with Cacher; for screenshot-to-code features, examine Pieces. For keeping a screenshot and the few relevant lines visible while you edit, FloatBoard can complement those tools. Try the task you actually repeat before committing your whole library.

sections.title: Choose the notes needed for the next paragraph
sections.html:
Start with the claim you are about to write. Choose the source detail you must verify, a short quotation if exact wording matters and the question that paragraph should answer. Leave the rest of your research in its original library or project folder.

A useful working note answers four questions: where did this come from, when was it published or checked, what does it actually say, and how will I use it? A floating note is a prompt to check the original source, not a citation by itself.

For an image you plan to describe, record its source and what detail matters. The screenshot above shows FloatBoard text cards beside image thumbnails, but a text-only writing task does not need images.

sections.title: Do not let a floating note become a lost citation
sections.html:
Use quotation marks for words copied exactly. Keep the original URL, author or organization and relevant publication date with the quote. When you paraphrase, compare your sentence with the full source passage; a short clipped phrase can reverse the meaning of a qualification.

For academic or citation-heavy writing, use a dedicated reference manager. Zotero integrates with word processors and can insert citations and bibliographies. FloatBoard does not replace that source library; it can hold a small visible working set while you consult Zotero or your documents.

If you are working with private correspondence or sensitive research, keep it out of screenshots that you share publicly. Only place material on the working board that is appropriate for that workspace.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about visible writing notes
sections.html:
How can I keep notes always on top while writing in Windows?

Open your notes app and use Microsoft PowerToys Always On Top to pin its active window, or use FloatBoard’s own pin control. Resize the note window so Word or your browser stays readable.

Can I keep reference notes beside Google Docs?

Yes. Google Docs runs in a browser window, so you can place a separate notes window beside it or keep a small FloatBoard window pinned above it. If your screen is narrow, a side-by-side layout may work better than an overlapping note.

Should I use a floating note or Zotero for research?

Use Zotero or another reference manager for the source collection and final citations. Use a floating note for the few facts or questions you need in view during the current paragraph. A source card on the board should always point back to the original.

How do I avoid accidentally copying source text into my draft?

Label exact quotations and your own paraphrases differently. Draft from the source idea with the original closed or beside you, then reopen it to verify accuracy and attribution before publishing.

At the end of the section, reopen each source and verify names, dates, numbers, qualifications and quotations. Move any lasting note into your source library or project document. Replace the temporary references with those needed for the next section.

Try FloatBoard with two source cards beside a draft, then decide whether a visible board improves your writing setup. If you mainly need to recover copied text, see the clipboard history guide; if you are comparing visual ideas, see the image reference workflow.

sections.title: How to copy and paste multiple items with Windows + V
sections.html:
1. Press Windows + V and turn on clipboard history if prompted.
  2. Copy a short piece of text, then copy a different one.
  3. Click where you want to insert the first item, reopen Windows + V, and select it.
  4. Repeat for another item. Check what was inserted before moving to the next field.

Microsoft documents a 25-entry history and a 4 MB limit per item, supporting text, HTML and bitmap formats. You can pin entries you want to retain. See Microsoft’s clipboard instructions, checked on 29 September 2026. These limits describe Windows clipboard history, not FloatBoard.

sections.title: Clipboard history or floating notes: which fits your task?

sections.title: Example: prepare a product listing without mixing up fields
sections.html:
Imagine updating a listing with an approved name, a short description and an image. The goal is to check each field against its source while editing. The following is an illustrative workflow, not a report of a measured time saving.

  2. Create a small FloatBoard text note with labels for the title, description and items to verify.

  4. Use the board’s pin control and position the window beside the editor. Switch back to the editor to confirm the note stays visible.

LISTING CHECK

Labels matter: two similar copied sentences can belong to different products. Keep one listing’s working set on screen at a time.

sections.title: Why is an item missing from Windows clipboard history?
sections.html:
First check whether history was enabled when you copied it. Then check the item’s format and size. An older entry may have been displaced by the history limit. Microsoft also notes that restarting clears unpinned history. Its clipboard support page explains pinning and clearing entries.

If a particular image does not appear, keep its original file and insert it through the destination app’s image command. Do not keep recopying a large file and assume the history panel will store it. If the entry appears but the pasted result looks wrong, inspect the destination’s paste options and compare against the source.

A visible reference is useful for checking the result, but it cannot repair an unsupported clipboard format or reconstruct information that was never saved.

sections.title: Keep the working set small and labelled

Before a new task, remove references that belong to the previous one. Preserve anything important in your project files first. Avoid copying passwords or other secrets into a board that might appear in a screen share.

Check the current FloatBoard plan limits before building a larger working set. A note containing a few labelled fields is enough to try this workflow. This article does not claim that FloatBoard provides Windows clipboard synchronization or an unlimited free history.

sections.title: Questions about clipboard history and floating notes
sections.html:
Does Windows + V show everything I have ever copied?

No. It is a limited history, not a permanent archive. Keep important material in a saved document and use the history for recent copied items.

Can clipboard history contain images?

Windows clipboard history supports bitmap content within its size limit. That does not mean every copied image or file format will be stored. Keep the original image when you need dependable access.

Can I keep copied text visible without repeatedly opening the history?

Put the relevant text in a note window. FloatBoard can keep a small text-and-image working set above other windows. If you already have the note in another app, a window-pinning tool may be enough.

What should I try first?

Try Windows + V for reuse. If the real problem is losing sight of instructions, try FloatBoard with one labelled note and read the clipboard workspace guide. For code and screenshots, follow the separate UI debugging workflow.

sections.title: Choose one result to reproduce

Before playing the tutorial, write down what you want to make: a responsive card, an image export or a spreadsheet formula. Record the tutorial URL and the software version used by the instructor if it is shown. Menu names and features can differ between versions.

For this example, suppose you are learning to build a card that changes from two columns to one on a narrow screen. You need the relevant breakpoint and layout rule, not a transcript of the whole video. Keep the completed exercise in your project folder.

The timestamp points back to the explanation. The actual-result line preserves your own observation. Keeping those separate helps you distinguish what the instructor said from what your project did.

sections.title: Follow a watch, pause, practise and check cycle
sections.html:
1. Watch one meaningful step. Stop when the instructor completes an action you can reproduce.
  2. Write the action in your own words. Copy a command only when exact spelling matters, and keep its source.
  3. Put the note in view. In FloatBoard, add your short text note, use the pin control and place the window beside your working area.
  4. Practise with the video paused. Return to your app and complete that single action.
  5. Compare the result. If a visual detail matters, keep one relevant screenshot alongside the note. Check small details in the original image.
  6. Record the outcome. Write what worked or the question to revisit, then advance to the next step.

Try this with one note and one image first. FloatBoard’s free plan has daily text and image limits, so use the board for the active step and your saved notes for the full lesson. The window does not need to contain every screenshot you take.

sections.title: What to do when the tutorial and your result differ
sections.html:
A menu item is missing: compare your software version with the lesson before trying unrelated commands. Note the version difference and consult that app’s documentation.

Your output looks different: compare at the same viewport size, zoom level or export setting. A screenshot without those conditions can lead you to fix the wrong thing.

The note covers a control: move or resize the note, or temporarily unpin it. If you constantly need to uncover the app, switch to side-by-side windows or pause the video more often.

You have too many unanswered questions: save them in the lesson document. Keep only the question blocking the current step in the floating note. For a reproducible interface problem, the code-and-screenshot debugging guide offers a more detailed evidence template.

sections.title: Turn the temporary note into a useful record
sections.html:
At the end of a lesson, save three things together: your exercise, the source URL with useful timestamps, and a short explanation of the step you can now perform. Move unresolved questions into that record before clearing the board.

Use screenshots you are allowed to retain and do not redistribute a paid course’s materials without permission. A screenshot can remind you where a control was, but your own explanation is what makes the note reusable when the interface changes.

sections.title: Questions about taking notes during tutorials

Should I write down everything the instructor says?

How can I take notes without a second monitor?

Pause the lesson while practising, use side-by-side windows when space allows, or keep a short note pinned above your app. Change the layout if it makes controls too small to use comfortably.

Does FloatBoard automatically transcribe or synchronize a video?

This workflow uses manually written notes, timestamps and selected image references. It does not depend on transcription, a video integration or automatic timestamp capture.

Can I use this for reading a written tutorial?

Yes. Replace the timestamp with the heading or section link. For longer reading and drafting, use the research notes workflow. To try the compact tutorial setup, download FloatBoard and start with a single next-action note.

This guide walks through both jobs with a four-photo example; FloatBoard is a visible reference board, not a full-size photo comparator.

sections.title: Decide what you are comparing before opening more photos
sections.html:
Choose one question: Which composition fits a project? Which lighting treatment should you study? Which of two exports preserves small details? The answer determines the layout. A grid of thumbnails can help you shortlist visual directions, but it is a poor place to judge sharpness, small text or exact colors.

For a fair comparison, choose images of a similar subject, angle and crop when possible. If the candidates have different framing or lighting, record that difference before treating it as a difference in the subject. Keep a link or filename for every original so you can inspect it again.

sections.title: Compare multiple local photos in Microsoft Photos
sections.html:
1. Open the current Microsoft Photos app and navigate to the folder containing your candidates.
  2. Open one photo, then use the filmstrip to select the other photos you want to view in multi-view.
  3. Compare the same feature in each image, such as a crop, reflection or edge detail. Return to a larger view before making a decision about fine quality.

Microsoft documents multi-view in the new Photos app as a way to compare photos and videos side by side by selecting items in the filmstrip. Its interface may differ if you have Photos Legacy or an older app version. This built-in option is a good starting point when the originals are local and you do not need them above a separate working app. Documentation checked on 1 October 2026.

sections.title: Use Windows Snap for two large images or browser pages
sections.html:
When you need to read details at a larger size, open the two originals in separate windows. These could be two browser windows showing source pages or an image viewer beside the app where you work. Select the first window and press Windows + Left Arrow; select the second and press Windows + Right Arrow. Resize the divider or use the available Snap layout to leave enough room for both images.

Microsoft’s Snap guide also describes dragging windows to screen edges or corners and filling the remaining space with Snap Assist. This layout is useful for checking two full-size views. If you keep switching among four candidates, narrow the set to two finalists before examining small details.

sections.title: Keep a short image shortlist visible while you browse
sections.html:
The screenshot above shows a real FloatBoard layout: four car images in a two-by-two grid, with larger source photos visible in the browser behind it. Use this kind of board when your task is to keep a few references in sight while you browse, draw or write—not to replace the original files or pages.

  1. Save each source URL or original filename in your project notes. Use images you are allowed to keep and share.
  2. Add two to four candidate images to FloatBoard using the image workflow in your installed version. Check the current plan limits before preparing a larger shortlist.
  3. Position the board where it does not cover the feature you are comparing, then use its pin control and return to your browser or work app.
  4. Give the candidates simple names in your project note—A, B, C and D—and write one useful observation for each. The labels belong in your note; this screenshot does not show labels on the image tiles.
  5. Open a source image at full size whenever a thumbnail leaves a question unresolved. Keep the final choice and its source in your project folder.

sections.html:
Suppose you are choosing a visual reference for an illustration of a car. In the screenshot, one image is an outdoor silver-car shot, another shows a blue car in a warm courtyard, a third has a dark convertible against a neutral background, and a fourth shows a bright yellow car in a courtyard. sections.title: Avoid four common mistakes when comparing image references
sections.html:
• Comparing unlike crops: match the subject and framing before drawing conclusions about proportions. A low camera angle can make a shape look different.
  • Judging exact color from a thumbnail: browser scaling, display settings and the source image can all affect what you see. Open the original in an appropriate editor when color accuracy matters.
  • Losing the source: write down the file path or page URL before closing the browser. A temporary board is not a project archive.
  • Reusing an image without permission: collecting a visual reference does not grant publication rights. Check the source and license before you put a photo in a public deliverable.

When a decision matters, record why you chose the finalist. For example: ‘Use the neutral-background image to study silhouette; keep the courtyard image only for warm lighting.’ That is more useful than a folder of unnamed thumbnails.

sections.title: Questions about comparing photos side by side

How do I compare two photos side by side in Windows 11?

Use Microsoft Photos multi-view for pictures in its filmstrip, or put two image windows side by side with Windows Snap. Choose Photos when you want a single viewer and Snap when you need separate windows or source pages.

Can I compare images from a website without making a collage?

Yes. Open the source pages in separate browser windows and use Snap, or keep a few allowed reference images in a small floating board while the browser stays open. You do not need to export a combined image just to make a decision.

No. This workflow uses human visual comparison of a small reference set. For pixel-level differences, synchronized zoom or duplicate detection, use a dedicated image-comparison tool and inspect the original files.

What if I need to organize hundreds of photos?

Keep those files in a searchable photo library or project folder. Use FloatBoard only for the few candidates you are actively considering, then save the final decision and source back in the project record. See the guide to organizing reference images for that distinction.

title: Best Way to Extract Text from Images & Review Beside Original Screenshots (Desktop OCR)
description: Extract text from screen captures with native OCR and verify accuracy side-by-side with the original crop on desktop without switching windows.
alt: FloatBoard displaying four image thumbnails beside a text card containing HTML reference text
caption: This FloatBoard screenshot shows a mixed image-and-text layout. It does not show OCR or the Windows text-extraction tools.
intro: Snipping Tool and PowerToys extract text from pixels; FloatBoard does not perform OCR. After extraction, keep the screenshot and a short corrected text note visible together while you check names, numbers and punctuation. This guide covers the Windows extraction steps and the verification workflow.

sections.title: Keep the screenshot as the source of truth
sections.html:
Before extracting anything, save or locate the original screenshot. Give it a useful name, such as shipping-error-2026-10-02.png, and keep it in the project folder. The copied words are a draft transcription; the image is the evidence of what appeared on screen.

If the screenshot contains names, addresses, account numbers or other private information, crop to the smallest relevant area before sharing it. For this guide, imagine a harmless sample image of a shipping form with the message “Pickup is unavailable for this address.” The example contains no real customer data. If the message exists as selectable text in the app, copy that text directly instead of running OCR on its screenshot.

Decide which part you need: the whole message, one field label or a reference number. A tight selection makes the later comparison easier. Keep punctuation and capitalization when exact wording matters, especially for error reports and instructions.

sections.title: Copy words from a screenshot with Snipping Tool
sections.html:
1. Display the screenshot at a readable size, or leave the original content visible on screen. Press Windows + Shift + S and select the relevant area.
  2. Open the new capture in Snipping Tool.
  3. Select Text actions. Select the exact words you need, or choose Copy all text for the whole snip.
  4. Paste into a plain note or draft field. Read the pasted result beside the screenshot before using it elsewhere.

Microsoft’s Snipping Tool instructions document the screenshot shortcut and Text actions, including selection and Copy all text. They describe this as optical character recognition (OCR) and say text recognition happens locally on the device. Interface labels can vary with the installed version, so update Snipping Tool if the option is missing and check Microsoft’s current instructions.

Copy all text is convenient for a single block. For a crowded dialog, select only the sentence you need; copying every label, button and footer can produce a confusing draft.

sections.title: Extract text already visible on screen with PowerToys
sections.html:
If you have Microsoft PowerToys installed and Text Extractor enabled, leave the screenshot visible and press Windows + Shift + T, its default shortcut. Drag a rectangle around the words. PowerToys copies the recognized text to the clipboard; paste it into a note, then compare it with the image. Press Esc to leave capture mode without selecting anything.

The PowerToys Text Extractor documentation covers the shortcut, selection and clipboard behavior. It warns that recognized text may be imperfect and needs proofreading. The default OCR language follows Windows language settings; the page also explains language packs if recognition fails for a language you need.

PowerToys is useful when the text sits inside an image, video frame or another visible app and you want a quick rectangular capture. Snipping Tool is the more direct choice when you also need to save a screenshot. Microsoft specifically recommends Snipping Tool for screenshot capture. Neither tool makes the OCR result an authoritative copy of the original.

sections.title: Compare the OCR result with the original, character by character
sections.html:
Put the screenshot and pasted text next to each other. Read the image first, then the extracted text. Start with the characters most likely to change the meaning: numbers, negative words, dates, punctuation, capitalization and lookalike letters such as O and 0. For multi-line text, confirm that OCR kept the lines in the right order. Do not silently “fix” a phrase from memory when the image is unclear; zoom in or return to the app that produced it.

Here is a fictional example of the shipping-form message. It illustrates a possible OCR mistake, not an observed result from either Microsoft tool.

Check each copied fragment against the screenshot
In the sample screenshotIllustrative OCR draftAction
Pickup is unavailablePickup is availableRestore “unavailable”; the missing prefix reverses the meaning.
for this address.for this addressRestore the final period if recording the exact message.
Try another delivery option.Try another delivery option.Keep this line; it matches.

Once corrected, label the note Verified against screenshot and keep the original filename or path with it. For a bug report, quote the corrected message and attach the screenshot as evidence. For a customer-facing response or an official record, verify the wording in the source system as well: a screenshot may be cropped, outdated or missing context.

sections.title: Keep the image and corrected text visible while you work
sections.html:
For a short task, two ordinary windows side by side may be enough: screenshot on one side, destination document on the other. If you repeatedly switch to another app, a small floating reference can keep the comparison nearby. FloatBoard lets you place an image and a text note in one visible working board, as the product image above illustrates. Add the screenshot as the image reference, then add a labelled text note with the checked wording and the source filename.

FloatBoard does not perform OCR in this workflow. Extract the text in Snipping Tool or PowerToys first, then paste the verified result into a FloatBoard text note if keeping it visible helps. Its clipboard history can help with recent copies, while the visible board keeps the image and checked note together. Save the authoritative screenshot and final text in your project files; a temporary board should not be the only copy.

If you mainly need to retrieve a recent copy, the Windows clipboard history guide covers that workflow. For a reference that must remain in view, check the FloatBoard download page. Use only material you are comfortable showing if you share your screen.

sections.title: Recognize the limits before relying on copied text
sections.html:
OCR can stumble on small type, low contrast, motion blur, unusual fonts, rotated text and overlapping interface elements. It may insert a line break in the middle of a sentence, join separate columns or omit a short word. The PowerToys documentation explicitly calls for proofreading; apply that habit whichever extractor you use.

A cropped screenshot can hide the preceding instruction or the label that gives a number its meaning. Keep enough context to verify what the text refers to, while avoiding unnecessary personal data. If a critical character remains unreadable, return to the source app, enlarge the image or request a clearer source. Do not guess at amounts, dates, codes or addresses.

Remember that copying OCR text changes its form, not its trustworthiness. Treat it as a transcription you have checked for your stated purpose. If an app supplies accessible, selectable text, use that source when possible.

sections.title: Questions about copying text from screenshots
sections.html:
Can I copy text from a screenshot without installing PowerToys?

Yes. Snipping Tool’s Text actions can extract text from a snip. Follow Microsoft’s current Snipping Tool instructions and check that your installed version offers the control.

Why did PowerToys copy the wrong words?

Try a tighter capture around the relevant line and enlarge the screenshot before extracting. Check the configured OCR language if the text uses another language. Proofread the result against the image; a second pass does not guarantee accuracy.

Is a screenshot or the extracted text better for an error report?

Keep both. The screenshot shows visual context; verified, selectable text makes the exact message easier to quote and search. Add the action that triggered the error, but exclude private fields. For a code and screenshot debugging example, see the UI bug guide.

Does FloatBoard recognize text inside an image?

No OCR feature is claimed here. Use a Windows text-extraction tool for recognition. FloatBoard can keep the screenshot and your verified text note visible together while you complete the task. Try FloatBoard if that visible reference would help.

title: How to Pin Private Notes on Screen During Teams & Zoom Calls Without Sharing Them
description: Keep meeting agendas, private talking points, and slides reference notes pinned right beside your camera without sharing them in screen share.
alt: FloatBoard window with text cards on the left and image thumbnails on the right
caption: This FloatBoard screenshot shows a mixed text-and-image layout. It is not a capture of a video call or the meeting-note example below.
intro: A personal checklist helps you remember questions during a call, while Teams Notes is the place for agreed decisions and actions. FloatBoard can keep a small prompt card visible beside the meeting window; it is not the shared meeting record. This guide shows a safe layout and what to check before sharing your screen.

sections.title: Decide what belongs in the shared record
sections.html:
Before arranging windows, decide which notes need to be visible to the whole meeting. A shared agenda, agreed decision, task owner and due date should live in the meeting record. Your private prompts might be a question you must ask, a figure to verify or the order in which you want to present. Do not leave the only copy of an action in a personal scratchpad.

Microsoft's Teams meeting notes guide says attendees can add an agenda, notes and tasks that others can see and edit. Changes appear live, and notes remain available after the meeting. In Teams, open Notes from the meeting controls. You can prepare an agenda from the calendar before the meeting too. Access can vary: Microsoft says external attendees cannot access or edit meeting notes. If your call includes guests, agree on a record they can actually receive.

Use a personal visible note for your own attention, not as a substitute for that shared record. This is a manual workflow published by FloatBoard.

sections.title: Arrange the call, shared notes and your prompt card
sections.html:
1. Open the shared agenda first. In Teams, select Notes and check that the agenda is the one for this meeting. Microsoft also documents an Open in new window option for meeting Notes, Chat and Copilot, so you can move or resize meeting content while the call continues.
  2. Make room for the conversation. Keep the speaker or shared presentation large enough to follow. Teams can reduce the meeting to a smaller window when you switch to another app; its controls remain available there. On one screen, avoid stacking so many panels that neither the speaker nor the task list is readable.
  3. Place your personal note. Add a short agenda or question list to FloatBoard, enable its pin control and put it beside the call. The FloatBoard desktop app provides a text-and-image board. A single text card is enough for most meetings; an image is useful only if you genuinely need a visual reference.
  4. Rehearse a window switch. Click the call, shared notes and the document you may present. Confirm that your note stays readable without covering mute, leave or share controls. If it blocks the meeting, shrink it or use a side-by-side layout.

sections.title: Copy a compact agenda and action template
sections.html:
Start with a note you can scan while somebody else is talking. The example below is fictitious. Replace every bracketed field before the call; leave the decision and action lines blank until the group confirms them.

MEETING: [topic] — [date]
OUTCOME NEEDED: [one decision or result]
AGENDA: 1. [question]  2. [choice]  3. [next step]
ASK: [one question I must not forget]
DECISION: [what the group agreed, or pending]
ACTION: [verb + deliverable]
OWNER: [one named person]
DUE: [date and time zone, or agreed milestone]
OPEN: [unresolved question + who will answer]

For example, a release-planning call might end with: Decision: move the checklist review to Friday; Action: send the revised checklist; Owner: Maya; Due: 9 October, 15:00 Casablanca time. That is a sample format, not a report of a real meeting. Use an explicit date when possible; “next week” becomes unclear after the call. If the group cannot choose an owner or due date, mark it pending and ask before ending the meeting.

Keep the personal card to one small working set. Put detailed background and final outcomes in Teams Notes or the team's approved project document. If you need to keep a source beside a draft after the call, the research-notes workflow covers that separate task.

sections.title: Capture the decision without trying to transcribe everything
sections.html:
During discussion, write keywords that help you ask the next question. When a decision sounds settled, read it back: “We are choosing option B for Friday's review. Is that right?” Record the confirmed wording in the shared notes. If someone volunteers to act, ask for the deliverable and date as well as their name. “Maya will send the revised checklist by 9 October” is usable; “Maya to follow up” is not.

Separate a proposal from an agreement. A useful shorthand is Proposed, Decided and Open. A proposal can remain on your personal card until the group resolves it; agreed work belongs in the meeting record. If the conversation moves quickly, write a short placeholder and return to it before the call ends. Avoid guessing what a quiet participant accepted.

Teams meeting notes let participants tag people in agenda and task items, according to Microsoft's instructions. If your organization uses that workflow, add the agreed owner there. A name on a private floating note does not assign a task in Teams.

sections.title: Check what people will see before you share
sections.html:
A visible personal board can also be visible to other people if you share the whole display. Before selecting Share, remove sensitive prompts, customer details and private links from the screen. Microsoft says Teams can present either an entire screen or a chosen window. Choose the window containing the material you intend to show when that fits the presentation, and inspect the preview or ask a trusted colleague what is visible. Do not assume that a pinned note is private merely because it sits outside your slide or browser content.

Pause before changing what you share. If you need to switch documents, stop sharing, arrange the new window and start again with the intended selection. This is a practical privacy precaution, not a guarantee that a particular operating system or calling app will always isolate every overlay. If an image on your board includes confidential information, remove or redact it before the call.

sections.title: Finish with an agreed record and clear your prompt card
sections.html:
Reserve the last minute to read out the decisions and action list. Confirm each deliverable, owner and due date, including a time zone where it matters. Record any unresolved point as an open question with the person who will answer it. Then check that the shared notes show the agreed version, rather than only your shorthand.

After the call, return to the saved meeting record or your team's project system to correct obvious gaps. Keep relevant links there. Remove obsolete or sensitive text from the personal board before your next screen share. FloatBoard's role was to keep the next prompt visible during the conversation; the persistent record belongs where your team expects to find it.

If this arrangement helps, download FloatBoard and try it with one short meeting card. For notes you copied earlier and need to retrieve, see the separate clipboard-history comparison.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about visible meeting notes
sections.html:
Can I keep my notes visible without a second monitor?

Yes. Reduce the call to a smaller view where your meeting app supports it, pop out its notes, or put a compact note beside the call. Keep faces, shared content and controls readable; if an overlay hides them, switch to side-by-side windows or a paper checklist.

Are FloatBoard notes the same as Teams meeting notes?

No. Teams Notes are collaborative meeting content for eligible participants. FloatBoard holds a personal working set of text and images on your desktop. Copy confirmed decisions into the shared record yourself; there is no automatic sync or transcription in this workflow.

Will a pinned note appear when I share my screen?

It may appear if you share your whole display. If you share a specific window, check the preview and the actual participant view before relying on that selection for privacy. Clear sensitive material before presenting.

What should an action item include?

Write a concrete deliverable, one owner and an agreed due date. Add an open question when a decision is pending. Confirm the wording aloud and place the final item in the team's shared notes or task system.

sections.title: Define the question before copying
sections.html:
Start with a task that needs both words and a visual. Suppose you are drafting a short accessibility review of a signup page. You need the specification's wording about error messages and a screenshot of the form state. The output is a recommendation, not a scrapbook of every page you opened.

Write the question in one line: Does the visible error tell a user what to correct? Then list the minimum evidence you need: a short source quotation, the page URL and date, one screenshot, and an observation in your own words. Keeping this list narrow makes it obvious when a copied passage is irrelevant or when an image lacks enough context to support a claim.

sections.title: Copy the smallest useful passage and its source
sections.html:
Select the sentence or paragraph that answers your question. Do not copy an entire article if one sentence will do. Record the page title, URL, publisher and the date you accessed it alongside the excerpt. If you plan to quote in published writing, confirm the exact words in the original page immediately before publishing and follow appropriate citation and quotation rules.

For the fictional signup example, a working card could say: Requirement — error text should identify the field and correction. Source: [document title], [URL], checked 5 Oct 2026. Keep the exact quotation in the source document if necessary; the visible card can be a short paraphrase with an explicit label. Separate copied words from your own conclusion. That prevents a quick note from looking like a verified quotation when it is only your interpretation.

A webpage may update after you copied it. If the wording is consequential, keep a dated source record in your research notes or issue tracker. FloatBoard is a visible working surface, not a web archive.

sections.title: Place the matching image where it can answer the question
sections.html:
Add one screenshot or licensed image that directly relates to the excerpt. In the signup example, capture the error state with enough of the form visible to know which field and action produced it. Remove names, email addresses and account data before sharing. Label the image with its file path or source URL and a short observation, such as after empty submit: error appears below email field.

Arrange the text card and image within sight of the document you are writing. FloatBoard can hold text and images in the same floating window; keep the window small enough that your destination app remains usable. The point is to stop repeatedly switching between a source tab, an image viewer and your draft while checking a single claim.

If the image is a photograph from the web rather than your own screenshot, note the creator and usage rights. The browser image-reference guide covers that separate source check.

Text-and-image check: Put one short copied passage in a FloatBoard text card with its page title and URL, add one related image, and pin the window beside the document you are reviewing. Label the passage as a source quote and write your conclusion separately in the project file; the board does not verify or cite it for you. Try a mixed FloatBoard working set.

sections.title: Write a claim that the two sources actually support
sections.html:
Now compare the visible evidence. A strong review sentence might be: After submitting an empty email field, the form shows “Email is required” beneath that field; the requirement asks for an error that identifies a correction. This sentence states what the screenshot shows and what the recorded source asks for. It does not assume that every error in the product behaves the same way.

Check for missing context. Could the screenshot show an older version? Is the copied sentence an example rather than a binding requirement? Was there a tooltip or announcement outside the captured area? Open the original webpage or application whenever the answer could change your conclusion. A floating layout reduces tab switching, but it cannot validate evidence by itself.

sections.title: Tell copied text, paraphrase and decision apart

This small structure avoids blending a requirement, an observation and a plan into one uncertain paragraph.

When you copy a sentence that includes a link, table or footnote, opening the original is essential. A plain text copy can omit those details. Likewise, text that looks like a heading may belong to a different section after it is pasted. Keep the board as a reminder to verify, not as the only available evidence.

Do not paste private customer text into a public screenshot or public document. Use approved data-handling rules for work material and clear temporary references when finished.

Clearing a clipboard history panel reduces accidental reuse of stale text, but it does not necessarily erase text pasted into documents, saved in apps, synced by other services, cached in backups or captured by screenshots. If you copied a secret, rotate or revoke it where appropriate rather than assuming the clear action made it safe. For private work, minimize copying sensitive material in the first place and check what screen-sharing participants can see.

sections.title: Capture screen crops at the speed of thought
sections.html:
When tuning 3D vehicle geometry, debugging responsive CSS breakpoints, or comparing API docs, you need immediate visual feedback. Switching out of your primary editor to open Snipping Tool or Paint destroys concentration.

FloatBoard bridges Windows 11's native Win + Shift + S hotkey directly to your floating desktop board. The moment your selection rectangle snaps, FloatBoard imports the buffer and floats it above VS Code, Blender, or Unreal Engine with zero latency.

sections.title: Keep text snippets and visual crops on one unified card
sections.html:
Visual references are rarely complete without technical specifications. When analyzing a vehicle chassis or styling line, you often need dimensions, wheelbase numbers, and torque ratings alongside the image.

FloatBoard combines visual cards with instant markdown scratchpads in the same floating window. Copy technical specifications, color hex codes, or terminal error outputs right underneath the captured crop. Everything stays pinned on top, moving together as one unified workspace widget.

sections.title: 100% offline clipboard protection
sections.html:
Unlike cloud-synced clipboard utilities that upload your screen captures to remote servers, FloatBoard is strictly offline. Proprietary engineering schematics, confidential client mockups, and pre-release automotive designs remain exclusively in your local machine's memory.

When you finish your task, one click clears the active working set. No traces remain on external cloud dashboards or secondary sync services.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions about Windows 11 screenshot capture
sections.html:
What shortcut triggers instant screenshot capture?

Press Win + Shift + S on Windows 11 or 10. Once you drag your crop area, FloatBoard automatically pulls the clipboard bitmap onto your pinned board.

Can I copy text directly from the screen?

Yes. Select and copy any onscreen text with Ctrl + C, or paste code snippets directly into FloatBoard's integrated scratchpad panel.

Does FloatBoard interfere with the native Windows clipboard history?

No. Windows + V history continues to function independently for historical recall, while FloatBoard serves as your focused, pinned foreground working set.
